title: Capstone: Build an End-to-End Production MLOps System
summary: This capstone lesson guides you through architecting and building a complete, production-grade MLOps system that ties together every skill from the course: containerization, automated training and inference pipelines, CI/CD, cloud infrastructure, and live monitoring. You'll plan the architecture, implement each layer, and produce a portfolio-ready project that demonstrates end-to-end ownership of a deployed ML service.
objectives: Design a reference architecture that connects data, training, serving, CI/CD, and monitoring components
Containerize a model service and reproducibly orchestrate training and inference pipelines
Provision cloud infrastructure as code and deploy a model behind a versioned, scalable endpoint
Implement CI/CD that automates testing, building, and deployment with safe rollout strategies
Instrument the system with monitoring for latency, errors, and data/model drift, with alerting
Package the project for a portfolio with clear documentation and reproducibility

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a model promotion gate in the training pipeline?
options: To only register a new model if it outperforms the current production model
quiz.why: The gate compares new model metrics against the production baseline and blocks registration if the new model is worse, preventing regressions from reaching production.

quiz.q: Which deployment strategy lets you roll back a bad model release without downtime?
quiz.why: Blue-green and canary strategies keep a known-good version available, so traffic can shift back instantly if the new release misbehaves.

quiz.q: Why is monitoring only infrastructure metrics (CPU, latency) insufficient for ML systems?
options: It misses data and model-quality issues like drift that degrade predictions silently
Latency cannot be measured in containers
quiz.why: Models can keep responding quickly while their predictions degrade due to data or concept drift; you need data/model-quality monitoring to catch this.

quiz.q: What practice makes infrastructure reproducible and reviewable in the capstone?
options: Clicking through the cloud console manually
Storing config only in your head
quiz.why: Infrastructure as Code defines resources declaratively in version control, making provisioning reproducible, reviewable, and auditable.

quiz.q: Name one statistical method you can use to detect feature data drift between live traffic and the training reference.
quiz.answer: PSI (Population Stability Index) or a KS test
quiz.why: Both PSI and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test compare distributions of incoming features against the training reference to flag drift.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what single quality most distinguishes a strong MLOps capstone in a portfolio?
quiz.answer: Reproducibility — a reviewer can set it up and run the whole system with minimal effort (e.g., one command).
quiz.why: Reproducibility demonstrates that the system is truly engineered and operable, not just a one-off notebook that works only on your machine.

body_markdown:
## Capstone Overview

This is the integration lesson where the individual pieces you've learned — Docker, pipelines, CI/CD, cloud infra, and monitoring — come together into a single deployed system. The goal is not to learn a new tool but to demonstrate **end-to-end ownership**: from raw data to a monitored, production endpoint that can be retrained and redeployed automatically.

Treat this as a portfolio project. Hiring managers want to see that you can connect components, make sound trade-offs, and operate a system after deployment — not just train a model in a notebook.

## Reference Architecture

A typical end-to-end system has five planes:

1. **Data & Feature layer** — versioned datasets (DVC or object storage), optional feature store.
2. **Training pipeline** — orchestrated steps (ingest → validate → train → evaluate → register) producing a versioned model in a registry (e.g., MLflow).
3. **Serving layer** — a containerized inference API (FastAPI + Docker) behind a scalable runtime (Kubernetes, ECS, or a managed endpoint).
4. **CI/CD** — Git-triggered pipelines that test, build images, push to a registry, and deploy with controlled rollout.
5. **Monitoring & observability** — metrics (Prometheus/Grafana), logging, and drift detection feeding alerts and retraining triggers.

The planes connect through artifacts: data versions, model versions in the registry, and container image tags. Each handoff should be reproducible and traceable.

## Step 1 — Scope and Success Criteria

Pick a realistic problem (e.g., churn prediction, image classification, demand forecasting). Define:

- Business metric and ML metric (e.g., F1, RMSE) with target thresholds.
- Latency and throughput SLOs for the endpoint (e.g., p95 < 200ms).
- A clear definition of "production-ready": automated tests pass, model registered, endpoint live, dashboards show traffic, alerts configured.

## Step 2 — Containerize the Service

Wrap inference in a FastAPI app, load the model from the registry, and define a `/predict` and `/health` endpoint. Build a slim image with a multi-stage Dockerfile and pin dependencies.

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.11-slim AS base
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY src/ ./src/
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "src.app:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
```

## Step 3 — Build the Training Pipeline

Orchestrate the steps so a single command (or trigger) reproduces a model. Validate inputs, train, evaluate against thresholds, and **only register** the model if it beats the current production version.

```python
if new_metrics["f1"] > prod_metrics["f1"]:
    mlflow.register_model(model_uri, "churn-model")
else:
    raise ValueError("Model did not beat production baseline")
```

## Step 4 — Infrastructure as Code

Provision cloud resources with Terraform (or equivalent): the container registry, compute (EKS/ECS/Cloud Run), networking, and IAM roles. Keep state in remote backend and never hardcode secrets — use a secrets manager.

## Step 5 — CI/CD Pipeline

Use GitHub Actions (or GitLab CI). On push: run lint + unit + integration tests, build and push the image, then deploy. Use a **canary or blue-green** strategy so a bad model can be rolled back without downtime.

```yaml
jobs:
  test-build-deploy:
    steps:
      - run: pytest
      - run: docker build -t $REGISTRY/model:$SHA .
      - run: docker push $REGISTRY/model:$SHA
      - run: kubectl set image deploy/model model=$REGISTRY/model:$SHA
```

## Step 6 — Monitoring & Drift

Instrument the service to expose Prometheus metrics (request count, latency histogram, error rate). Add a drift job that compares incoming feature distributions to the training reference (e.g., PSI or KS test with Evidently). Wire alerts: high latency, error spikes, or drift above threshold should notify the team and optionally trigger retraining.

## Step 7 — Document for Your Portfolio

A strong README includes: architecture diagram, how to run locally, how CI/CD deploys, screenshots of dashboards, and a section on trade-offs and what you'd improve. Reproducibility (one-command setup) is what separates a great capstone from an average one.

## Common Pitfalls

- Skipping the model gate, so worse models get promoted.
- No rollback plan — deploys become risky.
- Monitoring only infra metrics and ignoring data/model quality.
- Secrets committed to the repo.
- A project that runs only on your laptop and can't be reproduced.

slides.title: Capstone: Build an End-to-End Production MLOps System
slides.sub: Combining containers, pipelines, CI/CD, cloud, and monitoring
slides.narration: Welcome to the capstone lesson. Everything you've learned in this course — containerization, pipelines, CI/CD, cloud infrastructure, and monitoring — comes together here. Our goal is to build one complete, deployed MLOps system that demonstrates end-to-end ownership and becomes a centerpiece of your portfolio.

slides.title: What 'End-to-End' Really Means
bullets: From raw data all the way to a monitored live endpoint
Reproducible: one command or trigger rebuilds the model
Automated: tests, builds, and deploys happen on git push
Observable: you can see and react to what happens in production
slides.narration: End-to-end means more than training a good model. It means the whole lifecycle is connected and automated. A reviewer should be able to trace data to a versioned model, to a container image, to a deployed endpoint — and see that the system is monitored and reproducible. That ownership mindset is exactly what employers look for in an MLOps engineer.

slides.title: The Reference Architecture
bullets: Data & feature layer: versioned datasets and storage
Training pipeline: ingest, validate, train, evaluate, register
Serving layer: containerized API behind a scalable runtime
CI/CD: git-triggered test, build, deploy
Monitoring: metrics, logs, and drift feeding alerts
slides.narration: Picture five planes. The data layer holds versioned datasets. The training pipeline turns data into a registered model. The serving layer exposes that model as a container behind a scalable runtime. CI/CD automates moving code and models into production. And monitoring watches everything. The planes connect through artifacts: data versions, model versions, and image tags — each one traceable.

slides.title: Scope First, Build Second
bullets: Pick a realistic problem with a clear business metric
Define ML metric thresholds and latency/throughput SLOs
Write a concrete definition of 'production-ready'
Keep scope tight — depth beats breadth in a portfolio
slides.narration: Before writing code, define success. Choose a realistic problem like churn prediction. Set both a business metric and an ML metric with target thresholds, and define service-level objectives like p95 latency under 200 milliseconds. Then write down what 'done' means: tests pass, model registered, endpoint live, dashboards and alerts working. A tightly scoped project done well beats a sprawling one done poorly.

slides.title: Containerize and Pipeline
bullets: FastAPI service with /predict and /health endpoints
Slim, multi-stage Docker image with pinned deps
Pipeline: validate, train, evaluate, register
Gate promotion: only register if it beats production
slides.narration: Wrap inference in a FastAPI app with predict and health endpoints, and build a slim multi-stage Docker image with pinned dependencies. The training pipeline should run as orchestrated steps that validate input, train, and evaluate. Critically, add a promotion gate: only register the new model if it actually beats the current production version. This single check prevents a huge class of production regressions.

slides.title: Infrastructure as Code & CI/CD
bullets: Terraform for registry, compute, networking, IAM
Secrets in a secrets manager — never in the repo
CI: lint, unit, and integration tests on every push
CD: build, push image, deploy with canary or blue-green
slides.code:
- run: pytest
- run: docker build -t $REGISTRY/model:$SHA .
- run: docker push $REGISTRY/model:$SHA
- run: kubectl set image deploy/model model=$REGISTRY/model:$SHA
slides.narration: Provision your cloud resources with Terraform so the infrastructure is reproducible and reviewable, and keep secrets in a secrets manager. Then automate the path to production: on every push, run your tests, build and push the image, and deploy. Use a canary or blue-green rollout so a bad release can be rolled back instantly without downtime. Safe, automated deploys are what make a system truly production-grade.

slides.title: Monitoring & Drift Detection
bullets: Expose Prometheus metrics: latency, error rate, request count
Dashboards in Grafana for real-time visibility
Drift jobs compare live features to training reference (PSI/KS)
Alerts on latency, errors, or drift — optionally trigger retrain
slides.narration: Monitoring closes the loop. Expose Prometheus metrics for latency, errors, and traffic, and visualize them in Grafana. But don't stop at infrastructure metrics — add a drift detection job that compares incoming feature distributions to your training reference using something like PSI or a KS test with Evidently. Wire alerts so that high latency, error spikes, or significant drift notify the team and can even trigger automated retraining.

slides.title: Package It for Your Portfolio
bullets: README with architecture diagram and one-command setup
Screenshots of dashboards and successful deploys
Document trade-offs and future improvements
Reproducibility is what makes it stand out
slides.narration: Finally, present your work. A strong README has an architecture diagram, clear instructions to run locally and to deploy, screenshots of your dashboards, and an honest section on trade-offs and what you'd improve next. The single biggest differentiator is reproducibility — if a reviewer can spin it up with one command, your capstone moves from good to memorable.

slides.title: Avoid These Pitfalls
bullets: No model promotion gate — worse models reach production
No rollback plan — every deploy is a gamble
Monitoring only infra, ignoring data and model quality
Secrets in the repo, or a project that only runs locally
slides.narration: Let's close with common mistakes. Don't skip the promotion gate, or worse models slip into production. Always have a rollback plan so deploys aren't a gamble. Monitor data and model quality, not just CPU and latency. Never commit secrets. And make sure the project runs somewhere other than your laptop. Avoid these, and you'll have a genuinely production-ready capstone.
